items.definition: The ability to follow and build an argument made of words.
items.example: His verbal reasoning was strong: he checked the contract clause by clause and found the gap.

items.definition: The ability to handle quantity, order and calculation.
items.example: Numerical reasoning is what she used to compare the two costs before signing.

items.definition: The ability to handle shapes, positions and how parts fit together.
items.example: Spatial reasoning is what let him find the leak from a drawing of the pipework.

items.definition: The general ability that shows up across many different kinds of thinking, usually written g.
items.example: The general factor explains why a person who is good on one test is often good on others.

items.definition: The share of the spread of scores inside a population that is attributable to genetic differences within that population.
items.example: The heritability estimate for a group of students says nothing about the cause of one student's score.

items.definition: What a person has actually done, as distinct from what the person could have done.
items.example: His achievement in the first two years came from long hours and good training, not from a rare ability.

items.definition: A comparison that carries a case the reader knows into a case they do not know yet.
items.example: The analogy is clear: the pipe is like a road, and the loss is the distance.

items.definition: What a person has when they can recall facts, use them to answer a question, and say why they hold.
items.example: He had the facts and the knowledge, because he could say why the pump behaved that way.

items.definition: The act of saying what makes two things different, so that the reader does not confuse them.
items.example: The distinction between the answer and the reason matters in every report.

items.definition: The ability to bring a fact back into the mind when it is needed, without looking it up.
items.example: My recall of the formula is good; my recall of the reason behind it is not.

items.definition: A link between two facts, so that one explains, limits or changes the other.
items.example: There is a connection between the load on the pump and the life of the seal.

items.definition: A shape that several facts share, which is easier to see than the facts themselves.
items.example: The same pattern is in all three faults: the seal starts to leak before the part fails.

items.definition: An account that says why a fact holds, in words somebody else can follow.
items.example: The explanation of the fault was better than the manual, because it said why the seal failed.

items.definition: A set of steps written in an order that another person can follow.
items.example: The method is six steps, and any of us can run it on a new fact.

items.definition: A statement of what to do in a case, written for the situation the author had in mind.
items.example: The rule says to tighten the bolt to a stated torque, and it says nothing about the old bolt.

items.definition: The case in which a rule does not hold, and the rule is not wrong.
items.example: The exception is written under the rule: never on a seized bolt.

items.definition: The situation in front of you, with its own conditions, not the generic one.
items.example: This case is not the case the manual was written for.

items.definition: The situation around a fact that decides what the fact means.
items.example: In the context of a night shift, that warning means something different.

items.definition: The way a fact bears on the question being asked.
items.example: The relevance of the log is clear once you know which question you are asking.

items.definition: Running an AI model on one's own hardware rather than through a company's hosted service.
Publishing the trained parameters of a model so anyone may download, run and modify it.
Running a trained model to produce one answer. Cheap and fast compared with training, and it is what happens when you press send.
items.example: Training cost a fortune; inference is what you pay for every time you use it.

items.definition: The chips, data centers and energy supply that make training and running large models possible.
The condition in which switching suppliers is so costly that dependence continues regardless of price or quality.
The network of hardware, software, standards and services that a technology depends on to function.
The use of pressure, ambiguity or emotion to move a person into a decision that does not serve them, without giving a real choice.
items.example: It was manipulation: he offered her two options and made the wrong one impossible.

items.definition: An honest attempt to win agreement, in which the other person is free to say no.
items.example: That was persuasion, not pressure: he explained the plan and left the decision to her.

items.definition: A push applied to a decision, usually through time or emotion, that makes the choice harder to refuse.
items.example: The deadline is pressure, but you can still say that you need more time.

items.definition: The removal of a real choice by force or by the threat of harm.
items.example: Sign the form today or lose the job — that is coercion, not persuasion.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that presents the decisions of other people as evidence for your own.
items.example: The offer came with social proof: nine out of ten customers chose the larger plan.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that puts the decision in the hands of an expert, real or claimed.
items.example: It used authority: the technician said the part was safe, and showed no manual.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that claims the supply is limited, so that waiting looks like a loss.
items.example: The scarcity was easy to check: the shelf held six, not two.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that shortens the time available for checking and deciding.
items.example: The urgency was built to stop a phone call: sign tonight or the price changes.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that raises the cost of a slow decision, so that speed feels like safety.
items.example: The fear in the message was plain: if you wait, you are the one who pays.

items.definition: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, and which is used as a reason to continue.
items.example: The sunk cost of the training was the argument for staying in the job.

items.definition: Attention, affection and gifts given far faster and further than the situation deserves.
items.example: The love bombing was hard to refuse: every message came with a declaration.

items.definition: A repeated attack on a person's memory and judgement, so that they stop trusting what they remember.
items.example: It was gaslighting: she was told her own account of the meeting was wrong.

items.definition: A small, easy agreement that is used later as the reason for a much larger one.
items.example: The free trial was the foot in the door: the yearly contract came next.

items.definition: Being cut off from other people without choosing it, and without the comfort that solitude brings.
items.example: Working from home every day turned into isolation by February.

items.definition: Pressure strong enough to take away a person's freedom to decide, in the sense used in law and in medical consent.
items.example: The form said the signature was voluntary; the manager's tone made that undue influence.
